report.source_text: A 46-year-old man, with hypertension and past history of cigarette smoking, presented to the emergency department (ED) on March 26 for symptoms consistent with upper respiratory infection (cough, sore throat, and fever). The patient had been put on azithromycin by the general practitioner 3 days before the presentation in the ED. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay on nasal-pharyngeal swab sample was negative for SARS-CoV-2, while a chest X-ray was reported as suggestive for mild interstitial pneumonia. Thus, the patient was hospitalized in a COVID-19 ward and eventually discharged 3 days after, afebrile and without signs of respiratory dysfunction.

For this reason, he presented to ED again on April 4, when another nasal-pharyngeal swab PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. report.source_text: Quickly after the introduction of anticholinesterase therapy and oral steroid, dyspnea and fatigue significantly improved. Moreover, the 6-minute walking test did not show arterial blood desaturation.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 46-year-old man initially presented with URI symptoms and mild interstitial pneumonia, testing negative for SARS-CoV-2. After discharge, he developed progressive shortness of breath, generalized weakness, and effort intolerance. Subsequent neurological examination revealed classic myasthenic signs including hypophonia, diplopia, ptosis, and proximal limb weakness. Serological tests for common myasthenia gravis antibodies (AChR, MuSK, RyR) were negative. However, electrophysiological studies (repetitive nerve stimulation) showed a significant decrement, consistent with a neuromuscular junction disorder. The diagnosis was further supported by a significant clinical improvement in dyspnea and fatigue, and normalization of the 6-minute walking test, after initiation of anticholinesterase therapy and oral steroids.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient developed new symptoms of shortness of breath, generalized weakness, and marked effort intolerance a few days after initial discharge.

Neurological examination on April 24 revealed slight hypophonia after sustained speech, slight diplopia, ptosis in one eye during sustained upward gaze, and slight weakness in proximal lower limb muscles (4/5 MRC).
Serological testing for antibodies against acetylcholine receptor (AChR), muscle-specific kinase (MUSK), and ryanodin receptor (RyR) was negative.
Repetitive nerve stimulation showed 15% decrement in the amplitude of compound muscle action potential in the right nasalis muscle while stimulating at low frequency (5 Hz) the facial nerve.
Dyspnea and fatigue significantly improved, and the 6-minute walking test normalized, quickly after the introduction of anticholinesterase therapy and oral steroid.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Multiple negative PCR assays and rapid Ig tests for SARS-CoV-2 (E001, E002, E004).
Serological testing for AChR, MuSK, and RyR antibodies was negative (E009).

remaining_uncertainties: Specific details on the long-term clinical course or maintenance therapy beyond initial improvement.
